title: Recursion, base cases and recursive progress
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C language rules.
Trace the example and explain data flow.
Identify common errors and boundary conditions.
Apply the concept in a small tested program.

understand.concept: A recursive function calls itself directly or indirectly. A correct recursive design needs a base case and a recursive step that moves each call toward that base case. Each active call has its own automatic parameters and local objects.
understand.whyItMatters: Recursion can express divide-and-conquer and naturally recursive structures, but missing or unreachable base cases can cause unbounded calls and stack exhaustion.
understand.analogy: Treat a function or pointer operation as an explicit contract between caller and callee.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for types, object lifetime, scope and linkage.

explain.narrative:
A recursive function calls itself directly or indirectly. A correct recursive design needs a base case and a recursive step that moves each call toward that base case. Each active call has its own automatic parameters and local objects.

When applying this concept, check declared types, preconditions, object lifetime and all control-flow paths. Compile with warnings enabled and test both typical and boundary inputs.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: factorial(5) calls factorial(4), then 3, 2 and 1. The base case returns one; results are combined while calls return. This example's result type has a limited range, so large inputs can overflow.

practise.guidedTask: Draw the call sequence for factorial(4) and the return sequence.
practise.independentTask: Write a recursive sum function. Define the empty-input case and explain how each call reduces the remaining problem.
hints: A recursive step must make measurable progress toward a base case.
Recursion depth consumes resources and may be limited by the execution environment.
Check arithmetic range separately from the correctness of the recursive structure.
